title: Convergent Representation in Vision-Language Models
one_liner: When image and text models learn together, their representations separate into different regions; the paper shows that aligning their shared underlying patterns matters far more than closing that gap.
lead: Imagine teaching a model to understand both pictures and words. You want it to learn that a photo of a cat and the word 'cat' mean the same thing. A natural approach: train the model so that whenever it sees a picture, it represents it as a point in space close to where it represents the matching word. But something surprising happens: even after training, pictures and words live in completely different neighborhoods of that space. This phenomenon is called the modality gap. The paper investigates what causes this gap and whether it actually matters for how well the trained model works on new tasks.

problem.h2: Why pictures and words stay separated
paras: In multimodal learning (learning from multiple types of data), the standard recipe is simple: represent each picture and its matching caption as points in the same space, then pull matching pairs close together and push non-matches far apart. This is called contrastive learning.

The puzzle: after months of training, this actually works—the model learns useful representations. But when you inspect the learned space, pictures cluster in one region and words cluster in a completely different region, even though they should be close. This separation is the modality gap. A beginner would guess this is a bug—that the learning failed. But the model still works well downstream, so what is going on?

callout.html: The paper proves that pictures and words separate into different subspaces (dimension collapse), but their underlying patterns align in a shared lower-dimensional layer that dominates downstream performance.

panels.title: 1. The setup
panels.caption: A model learns from pictures and captions together, pulling close matches near each other.

panels.title: 2. The problem appears
panels.caption: After training, pictures and words end up in different neighborhoods; the gap is real and persistent.

panels.title: 3. A shared pattern emerges
panels.viz_args: Both collapse into same lower-layer patterns
panels.caption: Below the surface, picture-representations and word-representations both use identical underlying structure.

panels.title: 4. Aligning the shared layer
panels.caption: The method strengthens alignment in that shared lower layer without worrying about the surface gap.

panels.title: 5. Better downstream performance
panels.caption: Models trained this way transfer better to new vision and language tasks.

steps.text: Show the model matching images and captions, pull them close in representation space.
The representations squeeze into lower-dimensional subspaces (like data fitting onto a plane).
Even though pictures and words occupy different neighborhoods, they activate the same underlying dimensions.
Optimize training to strengthen agreement on those shared lower-dimensional patterns.
Test the model on new tasks; shared alignment predicts performance better than gap size, because downstream models use only the principal directions that matter.

paras: The paper changes what the learning algorithm optimizes for. Standard contrastive learning tries to pull matching pairs close to shrink the distance between pictures and words. The new method (Shared Space Alignment) instead optimizes the alignment of the basis vectors—the fundamental directions—that picture and word representations use, even if their centers stay far apart.

hidden.name: alignment of shared basis vectors
paras: When many data points are represented as high-dimensional numbers, they often do not actually use all those dimensions equally. Instead, most of the structure lives in a smaller subset of directions—like a cloud of points that mostly spreads along a few axes. This lower-dimensional subspace is the 'shared basis'.

The paper measures how well the basis vectors (the fundamental directions) used by image representations agree with those used by text representations. Even if the two modalities occupy different regions of space, if they use the same underlying axes, a model trained on one modality can transfer to the other.

heat.caption: Darker dimensions are used more. Image and text agree strongly on dim 1; agreement fades at lower importance; unused tail dims stay dark.

reads.html: The model learns by rotating its internal dimensions. Images and words both rotate to use the same strong dimensions, even though they sit in different corners of the space.

When representations collapse into dimension-reduced subspaces, their dominant eigenvectors (the directions of most variance) must align for downstream transfer, independent of the distance between cluster centers.

mechanism.h2: Why aligning the shared basis works
paras: High-dimensional spaces are enormous, so data almost never spreads evenly in all directions. Instead, it clumps into lower-dimensional structures, like how a pile of leaves lies mostly on a table even though the table exists in a three-dimensional room. When image and text data are represented this way, each modality collapses into its own thin subspace—but these subspaces overlap.

A downstream model (say, a classifier trained on top of the representations) uses only the relevant directions. If the image representations and text representations agree on which directions are important, then a classifier trained on images will work on text, and vice versa. The actual distance between the two clusters matters far less than the alignment of their shared principal axes.

Standard contrastive learning tries to shrink that distance directly, which is hard—it pushes the model toward contradictory goals. The new method instead optimizes the alignment of the basis vectors. This is easier because it does not require the representations to move to the same location; it only requires them to 'point the same way' in their most informative directions.

stages.s: Measure agreement between image and text axes
Aligned representations; downstream models transfer better because they can reuse the same important directions.

math.words: Loss equals: contrastive loss (pull matching pairs closer, push non-matches apart) plus a weight times the basis-mismatch penalty (measure how differently image and text use their principal directions).
symbols: standard contrastive loss pulling matching image-text pairs near and non-matches far
a score from 0 to 1 measuring how well the principal axes (eigenvectors) of image representations match text representations; 1 means perfect agreement
a weight controlling how much to favor basis alignment relative to standard contrastive learning
the set of principal directions (eigenvectors) used by image representations
the set of principal directions (eigenvectors) used by text representations

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose image representations use principal directions [1, 0], [0, 1] with importance weights [8.0, 2.0].
Text representations use principal directions [1, 0], [0, 1] with importance weights [7.9, 2.1].
The basis vectors are identical, so alignment score = 1.0, penalty = 0.
Now suppose text instead uses directions [0.9, 0.1], [−0.1, 0.9] (rotated 6 degrees).
The dot product of first axes: [1,0] · [0.9,0.1] = 0.9, so alignment drops to 0.9, penalty = 0.1.
With lambda = 1, loss increases by 0.1, nudging training toward better alignment.

math.note: The equation does not require image and text to occupy the same region, only that their principal axes point the same direction.

Transfer to new language task (pretrain on images+captions)
charts.note: Better transfer: aligning the basis vectors makes features reusable across modalities without closing the surface gap, because downstream models rely on the principal directions, not on cluster proximity.

items.b: Basis estimation fails with too few samples.
items.html: Computing reliable principal axes requires seeing many examples. On tiny datasets the principal directions are noisy, and the alignment score becomes meaningless.
In extremely high-dimensional spaces (millions of dimensions), most of the space is noise. If the model has more adjustable numbers than training examples, the apparent alignment might be accidental.

items.b: Modality representations are not actually low-rank.
items.html: If images and text genuinely need all their dimensions (no underlying subspace), then dimension collapse does not happen, and basis alignment becomes irrelevant.
When two modalities are learned together with basis alignment, downstream models trained on one modality transfer naturally to the other, even though the raw representations live far apart.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small contrastive learner on paired image-caption data (e.g., 10,000 image-text pairs from a standard dataset). Train one version with standard contrastive loss only, and a second with the Shared Space Alignment loss. After training, measure: (1) the distance between image and text cluster centers (the modality gap), (2) the alignment of their principal axes (eigenvector dot products), (3) how well a classifier trained on image representations transfers to text data and vice versa. Plot alignment score and transfer accuracy together. The demo must make visible that high alignment predicts transfer even when the modality gap remains large.
demo.closing: The core finding: basis alignment, not gap closure, determines whether features learned from one modality work for the other.
